metadata.note: The Santa Fe's Kansas City - Galveston main line - the north-south route that the Texas Chief ran and that the map was missing entirely between Wichita and Temple. Four companies built it and all four were Santa Fe: the Wichita and Southwestern (Newton - Wichita, 1872), the Cowley, Sumner and Fort Smith (Wichita - Arkansas City, 1879-80), the Southern Kansas Railway (Arkansas City - Purcell across Indian Territory, 1886-87) and the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe (Fort Worth - Purcell, 1887, on top of its own 1881 Galveston - Fort Worth main). The last gap closed at Purcell in the spring of 1887 and through Kansas City - Galveston trains began that June. Kansas City - Emporia - Newton is not drawn again here: it is the Santa Fe transcontinental main already drawn in data/santa_fe_chief.geojson, and Temple - Houston is already drawn in data/gulf_colorado_santa_fe_railway.geojson. What this layer adds is Newton - Wichita - Arkansas City - Oklahoma City - Purcell - Fort Worth - Temple, the Houston - Galveston tail, and the two through trains that tie the whole thing together. Ownership colouring follows the existing GC&SF layer: pre-1887 independent GC&SF in #6C7BC4, everything Santa Fe-controlled in #003DA5, Amtrak in #1c4e80. The Santa Fe-era features stop in 1971 because Amtrak, not the Santa Fe, ran the trains after May 1 1971; the Amtrak years to October 8 1979 are the Lone Star feature.

Relations used: 1431363 BNSF Arkansas City Subdivision (Newton-Wichita-Winfield-Arkansas City), 1451445 BNSF Red Rock Subdivision (Arkansas City-Oklahoma City-Purcell-Gainesville), 1458513 BNSF Fort Worth Subdivision (Gainesville-Fort Worth-Cleburne-Temple), 7403491 BNSF Mykawa Subdivision and 7461034 BNSF Galveston Subdivision (Houston-Alvin-Galveston). All five are the Santa Fe's own alignments, still in freight use under BNSF.
not_yet_sourced: Train counts before 1948: every pre-1948 headway_min in this file is a flat estimate. No period Official Guide or Santa Fe public timetable was consulted, so the 1887-1948 service level over the Gulf route is genuinely unknown here.

Sources conflict on when the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe met the Southern Kansas at Purcell - Wikipedia says April 26 1887, the TSHA handbook April 27 1887 - and on the Cowley, Sumner and Fort Smith opening dates at Winfield and Arkansas City (September 29 / December 31 1879 versus October 1 1879 / January 2 1880). Both conflicts are recorded in the segment notes; neither is resolved.

The 1948 Texas Chief schedule is given as 26h15 by Wikipedia but works out at about 27h15 in the March 1967 timetable; whether the train was slowed over its life or one figure is simply wrong has not been checked.

No period map was checked for realignments, so every feature draws present-day BNSF alignment for eras as far back as 1872. The Houston terminal approach is known to differ - see the Houston - Galveston features' geometry_quality.
Whether any passenger service other than the Texas Chief and its predecessors used the Newton - Wichita - Arkansas City segment after 1948 has not been checked.
metadata.passenger_only_rule: Every feature ends at the end of passenger service, not at the end of the railroad. Houston - Galveston stops in 1967, everything else in 1971 for the Santa Fe-operated features and 1979 for the Amtrak one. BNSF still runs freight over all of it; that is not drawn. The Oklahoma City - Fort Worth portion has had passenger service again since 1999 (Heartland Flyer), drawn in data/amtrak.geojson rather than here.

properties.speed_source: March 1967 Texas Chief timetable: Newton 4:55A to Wichita 5:35A, 27.2 timetable miles in 40 minutes = 41 mph = 66 km/h. That is one late-era snapshot; 1870s-90s running over this branch was slower.

segments.note: Built as the Wichita and Southwestern Railroad, incorporated June 22 1871 on $200,000 of Sedgwick County bonds and operated by the Santa Fe from the day it opened; the first passenger train reached Wichita on the night of May 16 1872. For its first eight years this was a 27-mile stub off the Santa Fe main line at Newton - the rails stopped at Wichita. headway_min is an estimate for a branch of that period, not a timetable figure.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1871 incorporation, the county bonds and the May 16 1872 first train are sourced; the 1880 end year is the date the line south of Wichita opened (see the Wichita - Arkansas City feature) rather than anything that happened here, and headway_min is an unsourced estimate.

segments.note: With the Cowley, Sumner and Fort Smith line open to Arkansas City in January 1880 this stopped being a stub and became the first 27 miles of a Kansas through route to the Indian Territory border. Still local Kansas service: the Santa Fe had no rails south of Arkansas City yet. headway_min estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: era boundary taken from the construction dates south of Wichita, not from a timetable for this segment. headway_min and the service description are estimates.

segments.note: From June 1887 this was part of the Santa Fe’s Kansas City - Galveston main line: the Southern Kansas Railway reached Purcell on June 12 1887 and met the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe coming north from Fort Worth, and through Kansas City - Galveston trains began running. Newton - Wichita carried the Gulf trains for the next sixty years alongside local service. headway_min is an estimate across a 61-year span.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1887 through-route date is sourced (see the Arkansas City - Purcell feature); no timetable was consulted for train counts over this segment in this era, and headway_min is an unsourced estimate.

segments.note: The Texas Chief, inaugurated April 3 1948, ran Chicago - Kansas City - Newton - Wichita - Galveston and was the train that mattered on this segment for its last two decades. Amtrak took the route over on May 1 1971; the ATSF-operated era ends there. Passenger service itself continued to October 8 1979 under Amtrak and is drawn as the separate Lone Star feature in this file. headway_min 1440 = the one daily train each way shown in the March 1967 timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the April 3 1948 inaugural is from the Wikipedia Texas Chief article; the one-train-a-day headway and the 40-minute Newton - Wichita running time are read off the March 1967 Santa Fe timetable reproduced at streamlinerschedules.com.

segments.note: Built by the Cowley, Sumner and Fort Smith Railroad - formed October 28 1878, construction from May 1879 - down the Walnut valley through Mulvane and Winfield to Arkansas City. segments.note: The Santa Fe’s line across Indian Territory, built by its Southern Kansas Railway affiliate: the first regular schedule ran Arkansas City to Ponca (later White Eagle), 31 miles, on November 29 1886; to Cow Creek half a mile south of present-day Perry, 59 miles, by January 6 1887; to Deer Creek - now Guthrie - in early February; and the whole 154 miles to Purcell by June 12 1887. Because this feature’s geometry is the complete Arkansas City - Purcell line it is drawn from 1887, not from the November 1886 partial opening. Guthrie and Oklahoma City both grew from construction camps on this line, and it carried the crowds of the April 22 1889 land run. headway_min is an unsourced estimate across a 61-year span.
sources: Segment-level: the November 29 1886 / January 6 1887 / February 1887 / June 12 1887 progression and the 154-mile figure are from the Cowley County historical society’s account of the Arkansas City depot; the Oklahoma Historical Society entry independently dates the completed Purcell main line to 1887. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: Texas Chief era over Ponca City, Perry, Guthrie, Oklahoma City, Norman and Purcell. Relations used: 1431363 BNSF Arkansas City Subdivision (Newton-Wichita-Winfield-Arkansas City), 1451445 BNSF Red Rock Subdivision (Arkansas City-Oklahoma City-Purcell-Gainesville), 1458513 BNSF Fort Worth Subdivision (Gainesville-Fort Worth-Cleburne-Temple), 7403491 BNSF Mykawa Subdivision and 7461034 BNSF Galveston Subdivision (Houston-Alvin-Galveston). All five are the Santa Fe's own alignments, still in freight use under BNSF.
properties.geometry_quality: Assembled geometry, not one trace. Chicago - Kansas City is the modern Amtrak Southwest Chief shape already used by data/santa_fe_chief.geojson: the same ATSF main line the Texas Chief ran, but a coarse GTFS-derived modern alignment (98 points for 449 miles), so nothing about its pre-1971 detail is verified here. Kansas City - Olathe - Ottawa - Emporia - Newton is traced for this layer from the BNSF Emporia Subdivision (OSM 1431383) and the Newton - Elinor relation (OSM 7764254): 183.5 traced miles against 185.2 timetable miles. That mileage is what settles the routing question - the train is often described as running via Topeka, but the Topeka Subdivision route traces 198.8 miles, 14 miles longer than the timetable allows, while the Ottawa line matches, so the Ottawa line is what is drawn. Newton - Wichita - Arkansas City - Purcell - Fort Worth - Temple is this layer’s own OSM trace; Temple - Houston is the existing data/gulf_colorado_santa_fe_railway.geojson trace. Straight-line joins between those pieces: 2.3 km at Kansas City, 1.2 km at Arkansas City, 0.1 km at Newton and 0.1 km at Temple. Total 1340 traced miles against 1352.9 timetable miles Chicago - Houston (March 1967); the shortfall is the coarse Amtrak shape cutting corners east of Kansas City. The train also ran Houston - Galveston until April 1967 - that leg is drawn as the two Houston - Galveston features in this file rather than being included here, so this feature is Chicago - Houston throughout its life. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 16 ruled segments totalling 220 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

properties.speed_source: Estimated. No Amtrak-era timetable was consulted; 76 km/h is the 1967 Santa Fe average knocked down about 10 per cent, reflecting the slower schedules Amtrak ran over the route. Treat as a guess.

segments.note: Amtrak took the Chicago - Houston train over on May 1 1971 and kept running it as the Texas Chief until the Santa Fe, unhappy with Amtrak’s standards, withdrew permission to use the name. headway_min 1440 = one train each way daily.
sources: Segment-level: the May 1 1971 hand-over and the Santa Fe’s withdrawal of the Chief name are from the Wikipedia Texas Chief and Lone Star articles. avg_speed_kmh and headway are estimates.

segments.note: Renamed Lone Star on May 19 1974. A Fort Worth - Dallas connection was added July 1 1975 and briefly dropped over the winter of 1976-77, when the train was combined with the Southwest Limited between Chicago and Kansas City; neither variation is drawn here. Discontinued October 8 1979, when it was Amtrak’s seventh most popular long-distance train - the last passenger train over most of this corridor. Amtrak returned to the Oklahoma City - Fort Worth portion in 1999 with the Heartland Flyer, drawn in data/amtrak.geojson.
sources: Segment-level: the May 19 1974 renaming, the July 1 1975 Dallas connection, the 1976-77 combination with the Southwest Limited, the October 8 1979 discontinuance and the ridership ranking are from the Wikipedia Lone Star article.
